specPoints.text: describe the evolution of stars with a mass larger than the Sun

primer.text: High-mass stars live fast and die loud: a shorter main sequence, then a red supergiant, then a supernova — the gigantic explosion that forges the heaviest elements — leaving behind a neutron star, or a black hole for the most massive of all.

lessons.title: Red supergiants
sourceHeadings: The life cycle of larger stars
lessons.opening: Past the main sequence, a high-mass star swells into a red supergiant. Compared with a Sun-like star it burns through its hydrogen in a shorter time, and where the solar-mass star fuses helium into carbon, the bigger star carries the build-up on to iron.
keyPoints: A high-mass star becomes a red supergiant after the main sequence.
Higher-mass stars leave the main sequence sooner — a shorter stay before the supergiant turn.
Helium fusion yields carbon in lower-mass stars; higher-mass cores carry the build-up on to iron.
As the supergiant expands, its surface cools and reddens.

low.restatement: Big star, brief youth: shorter main sequence, then the red supergiant swelling.
low.analogy: A fireworks rocket versus a candle: the bigger the charge, the brighter and the shorter the show.
low.examPointer: Contrast pairs score: solar-mass/carbon versus high-mass/iron.

medium.restatement: Mass drives both the clock and the chemistry: shorter main sequence, helium fused beyond carbon up to iron.
medium.analogy: A bigger bonfire: hotter core, faster consumption, larger glow.
medium.examPointer: 'Red supergiant' is one hyphenated concept — write it exactly.

check.stem: Compared with the Sun, a high-mass star's main sequence life is…

options.explanation: Bigger stars burn brighter and faster.
More fuel, far faster burning — the lifetime shortens.
Mass changes the lifetime.
The comparison is a standard fact.

check.stem: Past the main sequence, a high-mass star becomes a…

options.explanation: The supergiant stage precedes the supernova.
That is the solar-mass stage.
Solar-mass endpoint.
Not part of this sequence.

check.stem: A higher-mass star fuses helium into…

options.text: even heavier elements such as iron
options.explanation: Bigger stars build bigger nuclei.
Carbon is the lower-mass product.
Hydrogen is the fuel, not the product.
Fusion continues to heavier elements.

check.stem: A lower-mass star fuses helium into elements such as…

options.explanation: Carbon is the quoted lower-mass product.
Iron belongs to the high-mass path.
Not a stellar fusion product here.
Helium is the fuel being fused.

check.stem: As a red supergiant forms, its surface…

options.text: expands and cools, turning the star red
options.explanation: Same physics as the red giant, at greater scale.
That is the collapse direction.
The star swells enormously.
Red signals the cooler surface.

check.stem: State the stage a high-mass star enters after the main sequence.
State how a high-mass star's main sequence time compares with the Sun's.
check.modelAnswer: Its main sequence stay runs shorter than the Sun's.

check.stem: Explain why a high-mass star's fusion reaches heavier elements than the Sun's.
check.modelAnswer: The larger star's core runs hotter, so its fusion builds helium into still heavier elements — iron among them — where a solar-mass star stops at carbon.

check.stem: Two stars leave the main sequence: one Sun-like, one much larger. State each one's next stage.
check.modelAnswer: The Sun-like star becomes a red giant; the much larger star becomes a red supergiant.

lessons.title: Supernovae
lessons.opening: When fusion inside the red supergiant can no longer continue, the core collapses suddenly and a gigantic explosion — a supernova — blasts the star apart. At the centre a dense neutron star forms, while the outer remnants are ejected into space as new clouds of dust and gas; the heaviest elements are forged here and scattered.
keyPoints: When fusion cannot continue, the core collapses suddenly and a gigantic explosion — a supernova — occurs.
The explosion's centre condenses into a dense body: the neutron star.
Outer remnants blast into space as fresh clouds of dust and gas — nebulae.
Supernovae forge the heaviest elements and scatter them into space.

low.restatement: Fusion fails → sudden core collapse → gigantic explosion → neutron star centre, nebula outskirts.
low.analogy: A walnut crushed in a press: the hard core stays as a dense lump while the shell splinters across the room.
low.examPointer: Carry the element story: heaviest elements formed in the supernova and ejected.

medium.restatement: The supernova is a forge and a delivery service at once: heavy elements made, then scattered into future nebulae.
medium.analogy: A bakery explosion that showers the street with fresh bread — destructive and generative in one blast.
medium.examPointer: 'Neutron star' at the centre and 'nebulae' from the remnants — two distinct products, two marks.

check.stem: A supernova happens when…

options.text: fusion inside the red supergiant can no longer continue and the core collapses suddenly
options.explanation: Core collapse sets off the gigantic explosion.
Hydrogen fusion is the stable phase.
Planets are irrelevant here.

options.text: the core slowly shrinks for a billion years
options.explanation: The collapse is sudden.

check.stem: What forms at the centre of a supernova?

options.text: a dense body called a neutron star
options.explanation: The collapsed core becomes the neutron star.
No new main sequence star forms there.
A dense body forms, not emptiness.
The giant stage is already past.

check.stem: The supernova's outer remnants become…

options.text: new clouds of dust and gas — nebulae
options.explanation: Ejected remnants seed new nebulae.
White dwarfs form in solar-mass deaths.
The remnants are clouds of dust and gas.
Only the most massive cores go further.

check.stem: Where are the heaviest elements formed?

options.text: during a supernova, then ejected into space
options.explanation: The explosion forges and scatters the heaviest elements.

options.text: inside a nebula before the star forms
options.explanation: Nebulae are clouds, not forges.
White dwarfs do not forge heavy elements.
Planetary cores do not fuse elements.

check.stem: The ejected supernova remnants may later…

options.explanation: The nebulae of ejected remnants can seed new systems.

options.text: collapse into planets directly without any cloud
options.explanation: The cloud stage comes first.
They persist as nebulae and new systems.

options.text: orbit the neutron star forever unchanged
options.explanation: They are ejected into space, not locked in orbit.

check.stem: State what a supernova is.
check.modelAnswer: A gigantic explosion that follows the sudden collapse of the core when fusion can no longer continue.

check.stem: Name the dense body formed at the centre of a supernova.
check.modelAnswer: A neutron star forms at the centre.

check.stem: Explain why a supernova seeds new planetary systems.
check.modelAnswer: The explosion ejects the star's outer remnants into space as clouds of dust and gas — nebulae — and those nebulae may later collapse into new planetary systems.

check.stem: An astronomer finds unusually heavy elements in a young nebula. State the likely origin.
check.modelAnswer: The heaviest elements are formed during supernovae and ejected into space, so a supernova likely forged and scattered them.

lessons.title: Neutron stars and black holes
lessons.opening: The supernova leaves a neutron star at its centre — but for the most massive stars the story continues: the neutron core keeps collapsing under gravity until it forms a black hole — an object of such extreme density that its gravity traps even light.
keyPoints: A neutron star forms at the centre of a supernova.
In the most massive stars the neutron star continues collapsing under gravity.
The continued collapse forms a black hole.
A black hole is extremely dense — its gravity traps everything, light included.

low.restatement: Supernova leaves a neutron star; extra mass crushes it into a black hole.
low.analogy: A fist closing: the bigger the hand (mass), the tighter the squeeze until even light cannot slip between the fingers.
low.examPointer: 'Not even light can escape' is the required black hole phrase.

medium.restatement: Gravity's final word: beyond the neutron star stage, collapse continues until light itself is trapped.
medium.analogy: A whirlpool: the heaviest drain pulls everything under, even the spray.
medium.examPointer: Name gravity as the driver of the continued collapse.

check.stem: For the most massive stars, the neutron star at the supernova's centre…

options.text: continues collapsing under gravity into a black hole
options.explanation: Only the most massive cores collapse that far.

options.text: turns back into a red supergiant
options.explanation: Stages do not reverse.
The core stays dense.
Collapse continues in the most massive cases.

check.stem: A black hole is…

options.text: an extremely dense object with gravity so strong not even light escapes
options.explanation: Both density and the light-trapping gravity are required.

options.text: a giant cloud of glowing gas
options.explanation: That describes a nebula.

options.text: a hole in the Earth's surface
options.explanation: Nothing terrestrial here.

options.text: a star that emits mainly blue light
options.explanation: Black holes emit nothing that escapes.

check.stem: What force drives the final collapse to a black hole?

options.explanation: Gravity crushes the core past the neutron star stage.
Magnetism is not the collapsing agent.
Fusion has already failed.
Repulsion pushes apart; collapse needs attraction.

check.stem: Which is true of light near a black hole?

options.text: not even light can escape its gravity
options.explanation: Light-trapping is the black hole's signature.

options.text: light orbits it as a satellite
options.explanation: The of-record statement is that light cannot escape.
Gravity overwhelms light there.
Escape is the issue, not speed-up.

check.stem: The endpoint of the most massive stars is…

options.explanation: Supergiant → supernova → neutron star, then black hole for the largest.
That endpoint belongs to solar-mass stars.
A mid-life stage, not an endpoint.
Nebulae form from remnants, not the core's fate.

check.stem: Name the two possible endpoints left after a supernova.
check.modelAnswer: A neutron star, or — for the most massive stars — a black hole.

check.stem: Define a black hole.
check.modelAnswer: An object of extreme density whose gravitational pull traps even light: nothing, light included, can escape it.

check.stem: Explain why the most massive stars end differently from solar-mass stars.
check.modelAnswer: Their collapsed cores are so massive that gravity keeps crushing the neutron star further, forming a black hole, whereas a solar-mass star simply settles into a white dwarf and cools.

check.stem: A dying star is ten times the Sun's mass. Predict its path after the main sequence.
check.modelAnswer: Red supergiant → supernova → neutron star, and given the large mass, likely onward to a black hole.

glossary.definition: The swollen, cooled stage of a high-mass star after its main sequence.
The gigantic explosion following sudden core collapse, forging the heaviest elements.
The dense body formed at the centre of a supernova.
An extremely dense object with gravity so strong not even light escapes.
